_about: Short, sourced summaries of policies on AI use in manuscripts, grant applications and peer review. The report shows the ones matching the document's context. Re-check the source before quoting: policies change. Primary pages that could not be opened during research are marked 'secondary'.

policies.summary: AI tools cannot be authors. Authors must disclose AI use and are responsible for all content, including the accuracy of references. Reviewers must keep manuscripts confidential, which can rule out uploading them to AI tools; the 2026 update asks for the tool and its purpose to be disclosed.
AI tools cannot meet authorship criteria; their use must be disclosed. COPE Forum advice: AI-detector reports can only assist human judgement, not replace it.
LLMs cannot be authors; use beyond copy-editing must be documented in the methods. Peer reviewers must not upload manuscripts into generative AI tools.
Among the strictest: AI-generated text, figures or images without editor permission are treated as scientific misconduct; reviewers may not use AI to write reviews.

From September 2025, applications substantially developed by AI are not considered the applicant's original ideas; NIH says it will use AI-detection technology, and AI-generated content found after award may be referred to the Office of Research Integrity. Six applications per PI per year.
Peer reviewers may not use generative AI to analyse or write critiques of applications: it breaches confidentiality.

Evaluation cannot be delegated to AI: no summarising, judging or drafting assessments, and no uploading of proposal material. Polishing the language of one's own report is allowed; 'AI first draft, then edit' counts as delegation.
Applicants must be transparent about generative AI use. Assessors must not use generative AI in assessment (language refinement aside) and must not factor in whether an application seems AI-assisted.
Applicants must disclose substantive generative AI use. Reviewers putting application content into AI tools breach their confidentiality agreement.
Researchers may use generative AI responsibly and transparently; evaluators should not use it substantially when assessing Horizon Europe proposals.
Hallucinated citations are grounds for rejection; LLM-written reviews violate reviewer guidelines (ICLR 2026 contracted an AI-detection screen).
